content: Rifampin has been associated with liver dysfunction, and fatalities have occurred in patients with liver disease or those taking rifampin alongside other hepatotoxic agents. Patients with liver disease should only use rifampin after carefully weighing the benefits against the risk of further liver damage. Studies in rodents have shown that rifampin, when administered at doses 2–10 times the maximum clinical dosage, significantly increased the occurrence of liver tumors (hepatomas) in female mice of a strain predisposed to spontaneous hepatoma development. However, no evidence of tumorigenicity was observed in male mice of the same strain, in another mouse strain, or in rats. Rifampin is not recommended for intermittent therapy. Patients should be warned against intentional or accidental interruptions in daily dosing, as rare renal hypersensitivity reactions have been reported when therapy was resumed after such interruptions. Rifampin has been observed to increase the requirements for anticoagulant drugs of the coumarin type, though the mechanism is unknown. In patients taking anticoagulants and rifampin concurrently, frequent monitoring of prothrombin time is recommended to adjust the anticoagulant dose as needed. Rifampin and its metabolites may discolor bodily fluids such as urine, feces, saliva, sputum, sweat, and tears to a red-orange hue. Soft contact lenses may become permanently stained. Patients should be informed of these possibilities. Rifampin may reduce the reliability of oral contraceptives in some patients being treated for tuberculosis with rifampin in combination with other antituberculosis drugs. Alternative contraceptive measures should be considered in such cases. Rifampin, when combined with other antituberculosis drugs, may also decrease the pharmacologic activity of methadone, oral hypoglycemics, digitoxin, quinidine, disopyramide, dapsone, and corticosteroids. Dosage adjustments of these interacting drugs are recommended. Therapeutic levels of rifampin have been shown to interfere with standard microbiological assays for serum folate and vitamin B12. Alternative methods should be used to determine folate and vitamin B12 concentrations in the presence of rifampin. Rifampin crosses the placental barrier and appears in cord blood and maternal milk. Neonates and newborns of rifampin-treated mothers should be carefully monitored for any adverse effects. Isoniazid therapy should be discontinued immediately at the first sign of a hypersensitivity reaction, and the patient should be evaluated. Isoniazid use requires careful monitoring in specific populations, including patients concurrently taking phenytoin, as isoniazid may decrease phenytoin excretion or enhance its effects, necessitating dose adjustments to avoid phenytoin toxicity. Daily alcohol users are at a higher risk of developing isoniazid-induced hepatitis. Patients with chronic liver disease or severe renal dysfunction should also be monitored closely. Periodic ophthalmologic examinations are recommended during isoniazid therapy if visual symptoms occur. Rifampin crosses the placental barrier and appears in cord blood, but its effects on the human fetus, alone or in combination with other antituberculosis drugs, are not well understood. Animal studies have reported an increase in congenital malformations, such as spina bifida and cleft palate, in the offspring of rodents given high doses of rifampin during pregnancy. The potential teratogenic risk in women of childbearing age should be carefully weighed against the therapeutic benefits. Preventive therapy with isoniazid during pregnancy should only be initiated when absolutely necessary, as the benefits must be balanced against potential risks to the fetus. Preventive treatment is generally recommended to begin after delivery due to the increased risk of tuberculosis in new mothers. Isoniazid crosses the placental barrier and is excreted into maternal breast milk. Neonates and breastfed infants of isoniazid-treated mothers should be closely observed for adverse effects. Isoniazid has been reported to induce pulmonary tumors in certain strains of mice.
